title: Adaptive Spectroscopy of Fast Two-Level-System Dynamics in Superconducting Qubits
authors: Fabrizio Berritta, David Pahl, Lukas Pahl, William P. Banner, Gabriel Cutter, Jan A. Krzywda, Spencer Weeden, Shravan Patel, Paul Buttles, Stanislav Eilhart, Michael Gingras, Bethany M. Niedzielski, Robert McDermott, Mollie E. Schwartz, Kyle Serniak, Max Hays, Jeffrey A. Grover, William D. Oliver
abstract: Parasitic two-level-system (TLS) defects are a major source of energy relaxation and temporal instability in superconducting quantum processors. Our sub-second adaptive spectroscopy reveals telegraphic switching of TLSs with a characteristic timescale of a few seconds and spectral diffusion with diffusivity $D \approx 0.9~\mathrm{MHz}^2/\mathrm{s}$. These timescales are about $3 \times 10^2$ times faster than what is observed in conventional nonadaptive spectroscopy, which typically requires hours of measurement time. We resolve such fast dynamics on a field-programmable gate array (FPGA)-based controller that enables measurement of frequency- and time-resolved relaxations with sub-second temporal resolution in flux-tunable superconducting qubits. We observe similar defect dynamics across multiple qubits in independently fabricated devices measured in different laboratories. We correlate TLS-induced fluctuations with gate-level errors using randomized benchmarking. Our results reveal a previously inaccessible regime of frequency-resolved TLS dynamics and redefine the timescales relevant to TLS-aware characterization and calibration of superconducting quantum processors.
summary: The research presents an advanced spectroscopic technique to measure fast fluctuations caused by Two-Level System defects in superconducting qubits. By achieving sub-second temporal resolution, they quantified TLS switching rates and spectral diffusion coefficients previously inaccessible. This work fundamentally improves methods for characterizing decoherence sources, which is vital for scaling quantum processors.
main_problem: Parasitic Two-Level System (TLS) defects are a major source of energy relaxation and temporal instability in superconducting quantum processors, making characterization difficult.
main_result: The authors revealed TLS dynamics on sub-second timescales via adaptive spectroscopy, quantifying telegraphic switching rates ($	au_{sw} \approx 2.2$ s) and spectral diffusion ($D \approx 0.93 	ext{ MHz}^2/	ext{s}$).
method: They employed an FPGA-based controller to perform sub-second adaptive spectroscopy, combining Bayesian parameter estimation with randomized benchmarking.
model_or_system: The study uses flux-tunable superconducting transmon qubits. The noise source is modeled as a two-state Markov process (telegraphic switching) coupled to the qubit decay rate ($\Gamma_1$).
key_observables: Qubit decay rate ($\Gamma_1$), telegraphic switching correlation time ($	au_{sw}$), spectral diffusivity ($D$), and gate infidelity ($\mathfrak{r}_g$).
important_parameters: Sub-second temporal resolution, characteristic timescales of seconds (vs. hours for conventional methods).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the TLS dynamics using a two-state hidden Markov model and assumes that measured fluctuations are dominated by these defects.
figures_summary: Figures show time-resolved maps ($\Gamma_1(f_q, t)$) exhibiting telegraphic switching; one figure correlates gate infidelity with estimated $\Gamma_1$ fluctuations across different TLS resonances.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the problem (TLS noise) to developing an advanced measurement technique (adaptive spectroscopy on FPGA), quantifying fast dynamics ($	au_{sw}, D$), and finally correlating these intrinsic defects with measurable operational errors (randomized benchmarking).
why_interesting: This work provides a crucial, high-bandwidth diagnostic tool for characterizing decoherence sources in superconducting qubits, directly impacting the error budget calculation necessary for fault-tolerant quantum computing.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks
